claims.text: Elevated-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed by processing-induced nanoscale precipitates.
The as-fabricated alloy has a supersaturated fcc matrix containing abundant nanoscale precipitates.
The nanoscale precipitates form during additive manufacturing.
The precipitates act as preferential nucleation sites for oxidation or reduction reactions.
Secondary-phase precipitation creates localized chemical inhomogeneities in the fcc matrix.
Precipitate interfaces accelerate local oxidation or reduction reactions.
Under oxidizing conditions, precipitate-associated reactions promote a porous, non-protective oxide scale.
Under H2-rich reducing conditions, precipitates promote localized selective-reduction reactions that compromise surface integrity.
Post-fabrication homogenization will dissolve or coarsen the nanoscale precipitates and reduce their number density.
Reducing precipitate density through homogenization will slow elevated-temperature degradation.
Under oxidizing exposure, homogenized samples will develop thinner or more protective oxide scales than as-fabricated samples.
Under reducing exposure, homogenized samples will show less internal reduction damage than as-fabricated samples.
Homogenization can reduce degradation while retaining the alloy's fcc matrix.
Retention of the fcc matrix preserves the alloy's beneficial strength and fatigue performance.
The proposed mechanism applies over approximately 700–900°C in oxidizing or reducing gas environments.
The proposed mechanism is applicable to high-entropy alloys with similar compositions and processing histories.
